borders.before: the lecturer's welcome, course framing, and lecture learning objectives
borders.after: the core genetic definition of cancer and the interplay of mutations and microenvironment
borders.caseForKeeping: Subtopic 1 is opening framing and administrative introduction, while subtopic 2 begins the substantive subject matter.
borders.caseForMoving: Subtopic 1 is clearly opening framing on its own.
borders.caseForRemoving: Opening framing should be kept separate from the substantive lecture content.

borders.before: epidemiological global variations and broad environment vs. genetics discussions
borders.after: specific infectious pathogens causing cancer, notably H. pylori, EBV, and HPV
borders.caseForKeeping: Subtopic 7 transitions directly from general environmental/genetic risk discussion to specific biological infectious agents.
borders.caseForMoving: Subtopic 6 is still discussing general epidemiological patterns across countries, whereas 7 begins specific biological agents.
borders.caseForRemoving: The overview of general causation and global epidemiology is a distinct conceptual topic from specific pathogen-driven oncogenesis.

borders.before: the detailed mechanism of Burkitt lymphoma driven by EBV and malaria
borders.after: dietary chemical carcinogens (aflatoxin) and metabolic activation forming DNA adducts
borders.caseForKeeping: Subtopic 8 finishes the infectious pathogen section, while subtopic 9 shifts to non-infectious chemical and physical carcinogens (diet, UV, smoke).
borders.caseForMoving: Burkitt lymphoma in subtopic 8 directly finishes pathogens, so subtopic 9 is the natural starting point for chemical/physical agents.
borders.caseForRemoving: Pathogens act via distinct viral/parasitic mechanisms compared to direct chemical DNA adducts and radiation.

borders.before: tissue-specific metabolic activation of carcinogens (beta-naphthylamine in bladder)
borders.after: asbestos, chronic inflammation, and the distinction between initiators and promoters
borders.caseForKeeping: Subtopic 14 introduces the fundamental distinction between tumour initiation (mutagens) and tumour promotion (microenvironment/inflammation).
borders.caseForMoving: Subtopic 13 is still examining direct chemical activation (beta-naphthylamine), whereas 14 begins promoter concepts starting with asbestos.
borders.caseForRemoving: The conceptual framework of initiation vs. promotion and host developmental susceptibility is distinct from detailing chemical adducts.

borders.before: summary of mutagenic vs promoter mechanisms and tissue/developmental stage susceptibility
borders.after: mutational signatures and genome sequencing methods for identifying carcinogen exposure
borders.caseForKeeping: Subtopic 17 summarizes the mechanistic principles of carcinogenesis, while subtopic 18 starts discussing testing and detection methods (sequencing, biobanks, toxicology assays).
borders.caseForMoving: Subtopic 17 acts as a summary of preceding biological principles, making subtopic 18 the clean start of methodologies.
borders.caseForRemoving: Experimental and epidemiological testing methods are a distinct major division from biological mechanisms.

borders.before: in vitro Ames test and toxicological assay limitations
borders.after: lecture conclusion, risk vs benefit summary, and applause
borders.caseForKeeping: Subtopic 22 is closing lecture framing and summary wrap-up.
borders.caseForMoving: Subtopic 21 is a specific assay (Ames test); subtopic 22 concludes the lecture.
borders.caseForRemoving: Lecture closings constitute their own distinct framing section.

insides.caseForDividing: Subtopics 2-4 introduce the concept of cancer, endogenous vs exogenous causes, and environmental examples, while 5-6 discuss public perception and global epidemiological distribution patterns.
insides.caseForKeepingWhole: Subtopics 2 through 6 together establish the overarching framework of cancer causation (intrinsic errors, environmental mutagens, and population-level epidemiological evidence).

insides.caseForDividing: Subtopic 7 lists various pathogen examples while subtopic 8 focuses on an in-depth case study of Burkitt lymphoma.
insides.caseForKeepingWhole: Subtopic 8 directly illustrates and deepens the topic of pathogen-driven cancer introduced in subtopic 7.

insides.caseForDividing: Subtopics 9-10 discuss aflatoxin and UV light, whereas 11-13 focus extensively on polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons and cigarette smoke metabolites.
insides.caseForKeepingWhole: Subtopics 9-13 all explore the direct biochemical mechanisms of chemical and physical DNA damage, adduct formation, and metabolic activation.

insides.caseForDividing: Subtopics 14-15 explain the Berenbaum initiator-promoter model, whereas 16-17 focus on host cell state and life stage susceptibility.
insides.caseForKeepingWhole: Subtopics 14-17 all focus on the non-mutagenic factors and host contexts (promoters, inflammation, developmental stage) that enable tumours to develop.

insides.caseForDividing: Subtopic 18 discusses mutational signatures, whereas 19-21 discuss classical testing systems (epidemiology, animal bioassays, Ames test).
insides.caseForKeepingWhole: Subtopics 18-21 all address the overarching question of how carcinogenicity is proven and detected using modern and classical tools.

topics.label: Course Introduction and Learning Objectives
topics.groupedBecause: It sets the scope for the lecture series and outlines the key learning objectives regarding cancer causes, environmental exposures, and methodologies.

topics.label: Cancer Etiology: Genetic, Endogenous, and Environmental Factors
topics.groupedBecause: It explores the fundamental nature of cancer as a multi-step genetic disease driven by a combination of intrinsic cellular errors, inherited traits, and environmental exposures.

topics.label: Infectious Agents and Pathogen-Driven Carcinogenesis
topics.groupedBecause: It examines how bacterial, parasitic, and viral infections drive malignancy, illustrated through the mechanism of Epstein-Barr virus and malaria in Burkitt lymphoma.

topics.label: Mechanisms of Chemical and Physical DNA Damage
topics.groupedBecause: It describes how radiation and chemical carcinogens undergo metabolic activation in the body to form DNA adducts and induce genetic mutations.

topics.label: Tumour Initiation, Promotion, and Host Susceptibility
topics.groupedBecause: It explains the distinction between mutational tumour initiators and non-mutagenic promoters, including the influence of inflammation and host developmental stage on tumour development.

topics.label: Methodologies for Detecting and Proving Carcinogenicity
topics.groupedBecause: It reviews the experimental and analytical methods used to identify carcinogens, including mutational signature analysis, epidemiological biobanks, in vivo models, and the Ames test.

topics.label: Lecture Conclusion and Risk-Benefit Considerations
topics.groupedBecause: It closes the lecture by summarising the environmental origins of cancer and framing exposure decisions in terms of risk-benefit assessment.
